terms.grammar: tempus est with an infinitive; the person, if named, as subject accusative or dative
evidence: Liv. 21.54.2: nunc corpora cūrāre tempus est
Cic. Top. 1.5: sed jam tempus est ad id quod īnstituimus accēdere (Lewis & Short s.v. tempus)
terms.comment: English “it’s time to” goes word for word: tempus est surgere, it’s time to get up. With a person: tempus est mē abīre (Cic. Tusc. 1.99) or tibi abīre (Hor. Epist. 2.2.215).

terms.grammar: tempus est with the genitive of a noun or a gerund; a verb with an object goes into the gerundive
evidence: Sen. Ep. 122.9: lūcet: somnī tempus est
Caes. BG 2.19.6: quod tempus inter eōs committendī proeliī convēnerat
Cic. Fam. 3.10.6: aliēnum tempus est mihi tēcum expostulandī (Lewis & Short s.v. tempus)
terms.comment: “Time for sleep”, “time for supper”: the thing in the genitive. A verb goes into the genitive of the gerund (tempus est dormiendī, it’s time for sleeping), and one with an object into the gerundive (tempus committendī proeliī, the time for joining battle). The two constructions differ a little: with the gerund tempus is the proper time or season for a thing, with the infinitive it is high time to do it (Gildersleeve & Lodge §428, n. 2).

phrases.english: now it is time to look after ourselves (food, a bath, rest)
it’s getting light: time for bed!

phrases.latin: quod tempus inter eōs committendī proeliī convēnerat
phrases.english: the moment they had agreed on among themselves for joining battle

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 35.
B. L. Gildersleeve and Gonzalez Lodge, Gildersleeve’s Latin Grammar, 3rd ed. (1895), §428, n. 2.
